questions.q: Which grep flag makes a search case-insensitive?
options: -v
-r
-i
-c
questions.explain: -i tells grep to ignore case when matching the pattern against each line.

questions.q: You want to see every line in access.log that is NOT a health check request. Which command does that?
options: grep "health" access.log
grep -v "health" access.log
grep -c "health" access.log
sed 's/health//' access.log
questions.explain: -v inverts the match, printing only lines that do not contain the pattern — exactly what filtering out noise requires.

questions.q: What is the difference between `sed 's/old/new/' file.conf` and `sed -i 's/old/new/' file.conf`?
options: There is no difference; both edit the file in place
The first only works on the first line; the second works on all lines
The first prints the changed result without touching the file; -i edits the file in place
The first requires root; -i does not
questions.explain: Without -i, sed sends the substituted result to standard output and leaves the original file untouched. -i writes the change back into the file.

questions.q: In awk, what does $2 refer to?
options: The second line of input
The second field of the current line, based on the field separator
The second file given as an argument
An environment variable named 2
questions.explain: awk splits each line into fields (by whitespace by default, or whatever -F specifies), and $1, $2, etc. refer to those fields by position.

questions.q: Why would you use `awk -F','` on a file instead of plain `awk`?
options: To make awk search recursively through a directory
To tell awk to treat commas as the field separator instead of whitespace, useful for CSV data
To count the number of commas in each line
To combine awk with grep in one command
questions.explain: -F sets awk's field separator. Whitespace is the default, but -F',' is needed to correctly split comma-separated data like a CSV export.
